eligibility.evidence: Sections 1-4: 16 open-weights Gemma3/Llama3 checkpoints complete human dialogues; linguistic accommodation/convergence is modelled on human accommodation work (Giles et al. 1991; Ireland et al. 2011 LSM; Niederhoffer & Pennebaker 2002) and compared with the original human turns. Paradigm is sociolinguistic rather than a classic cognitive task, so E2 is borderline.

A.title: Do language models accommodate their users? A study of linguistic convergence
A.venue: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL 2026, Long Papers)

paradigms.name: Linguistic accommodation (convergence) in dialogue completion: model replaces one speaker's turns; convergence to preceding turn scored on utterance length, LIWC function-word agreement, proper-noun overlap, token novelty vs random-turn control and original human turn
paradigms.source_paper: Ireland et al. 2011; Niederhoffer & Pennebaker 2002; Giles et al. 1991

D.population: Original human speakers in DailyDialog (English learners' written dialogues), NPR interview transcripts, Movie Corpus scripts; number of speakers not stated
D.metric: Same four stylometric convergence scores computed on the original human turn (human baseline) versus random-turn baseline

E.headline: Models converge strongly to conversational style, often over-converging relative to humans; instruction-tuned and larger models converge less, and underlying mechanisms probably differ from human accommodation.

G.notes: Four metrics and three corpora are reported with no single headline row; extractor chose Token Novelty on DailyDialog because Table 5 gives a per-model test against humans. LIWC and utterance-length rows would give different labels (e.g. Gemma 27B IT below random on LIWC). Bold significance markers lost in conversion. Human baseline is corpus text, not participants; sampling parameters tuned on Movie corpus.
